title: Heritage walk in Jaisalmer: the living fort, havelis and lakes
seo_title: Heritage Walk in Jaisalmer: Fort, Havelis, Historical Places
meta_description: Plan a heritage walk in Jaisalmer: the living fort (a UNESCO hill fort), Jain temples, Patwon ki Haveli, Gadisar Lake, Bada Bagh, Kuldhara and local museums.
summary: A heritage walk in Jaisalmer goes through the sandstone fort founded by Rawal Jaisal in 1156, still lived in today, with its palace and Jain temples, then down to the merchant havelis such as Patwon ki Haveli and to Gadisar Lake. Bada Bagh, Kuldhara and Lodurva are short drives away.

paras: Jaisalmer Fort is one of the six Hill Forts of Rajasthan inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2013, and it is unusual among them because people still live inside it. Several thousand residents, shops, temples and guesthouses share the walls with the palace. That makes the fort both a monument and a neighbourhood, with all the pressures this brings: water, drainage, and the weight of new building on old foundations.

The city below grew rich on caravan trade across the Thar, and its merchant families spent that wealth on havelis with some of the finest stone carving in India. For students, Jaisalmer is a lesson in how trade routes create cities and how cities fade when routes change.

Rawal Jaisal of the Bhati Rajputs founded the fort on Trikuta hill in 1156, moving from the older capital at Lodurva, about 15 kilometres north-west. Lodurva's rebuilt Jain temple marks that earlier settlement. The fort faced several sieges in the medieval period and the state later made terms with the Mughals and, in 1818, with the British.

From the 15th to the 19th century Jaisalmer sat on caravan routes linking Sindh, Gujarat, Central Asia and the Ganga plain. Jain and Hindu merchant families such as the Patwas built havelis in the town from the late 18th and 19th centuries. The Jain temples inside the fort, built mostly between the 12th and 16th centuries, hold a famous manuscript library, the Jinabhadra Suri Gyan Bhandar, with palm-leaf and paper manuscripts; see [Indian manuscripts](indian-manuscripts.html) for background.

The rise of sea trade through Bombay in the 19th century, and the closing of the border in 1947, cut the caravan routes. Jaisalmer declined until tourism and the army revived it from the 1960s onward. Kuldhara, an abandoned village of the Paliwal Brahmins about 18 kilometres away, shows another side of desert history: settlements that rose and emptied with water and politics.

sections.h2: What you see on a Jaisalmer heritage walk
paras: The walk enters the fort through a series of gates (Akhai Pol, Suraj Pol, Ganesh Pol, Hawa Pol) to the main square, Dussehra Chowk, in front of the Raj Mahal. Inside the palace, now a museum, look at the jharokhas and the view over the town. The seven interconnected Jain temples are a highlight of yellow sandstone carving; check visiting hours, which are usually limited to the morning.

Leaving the fort, the route reaches Patwon ki Haveli, a group of five connected havelis built in the first half of the 19th century, then Nathmal ki Haveli and Salim Singh ki Haveli, a minister's mansion with a distinctive projecting top floor. The walk ends at Gadisar Lake, a 14th century reservoir with ghats, chhatris and the Tilon ki Pol gateway. Our guides to [forts of India](forts-of-india.html) and [heritage conservation in India](heritage-conservation-in-india.html) explain the fort's conservation problems.

sections.h2: Planning a Jaisalmer heritage walk for schools and groups
paras: The fort and havelis are close together and can be walked in about three hours; the fort lanes are narrow and stepped, so groups larger than 25 should split. Start at sunrise in summer. Bada Bagh, Kuldhara and Lodurva need a vehicle and fit an afternoon. Desert camp outings are popular but are not part of a heritage programme.

Jaisalmer walks are arranged for your group and planned with you. Jaisalmer is one of the forts in the [Forts of Rajasthan study tour](forts-of-rajasthan.html), and a lecture on [climate change and ancient settlements](climate-change-and-ancient-settlements.html) is a strong preparation for Kuldhara. A [documentation workshop](recording-the-past-a-documentation-workshop.html) suits college groups who want to record a haveli facade.

stops.name: Jaisalmer Fort gates
stops.note: Akhai Pol, Suraj Pol, Ganesh Pol and Hawa Pol, climbing in turns to defend the approach.

stops.name: Dussehra Chowk
stops.note: Main square inside the fort in front of the palace.

stops.name: Raj Mahal (Fort Palace Museum)
stops.note: Royal palace with jharokhas, now a museum with arms, coins and royal objects.

stops.name: Jain temples in the fort
stops.note: Seven connected temples with fine yellow sandstone carving; visiting hours are limited.

stops.name: Laxminath Temple
stops.note: Hindu temple inside the fort, still in daily worship.

stops.name: Patwon ki Haveli
stops.note: Five connected merchant havelis with carved facades; part is a museum.

stops.name: Nathmal ki Haveli
stops.note: A prime minister's haveli carved by two brothers, each working on one half.

stops.name: Salim Singh ki Haveli
stops.note: Minister's mansion with a projecting top storey and peacock-shaped brackets.

stops.name: Gadisar Lake
stops.note: Reservoir with ghats, shrines and the Tilon ki Pol gate; the town's main water source for centuries.

stops.name: Bada Bagh
stops.note: Royal cenotaphs (chhatris) of the Bhati rulers north of the city; vehicle needed.

stops.name: Lodurva
stops.period: Earlier capital; Jain temple rebuilt 20th century
stops.note: Site of the capital before 1156, with a carved Jain temple; vehicle needed.

stops.name: Kuldhara
stops.note: Abandoned Paliwal village with house plinths and a temple; vehicle needed.

museums.name: Fort Palace Museum
museums.note: In the Raj Mahal, with royal objects, coins, sculpture and views from the palace roof.

museums.name: Patwon ki Haveli museum
museums.note: Restored rooms showing how a merchant family lived.

museums.name: Government Museum, Jaisalmer
museums.note: Small collection of fossils, sculpture and local archaeology, including desert fossils from Akal.

best_time: November to February. Summer temperatures are extreme; the monsoon is short and light.

faq.q: What are the main historical places in Jaisalmer?
faq.a: Jaisalmer Fort with its palace and Jain temples, Patwon ki Haveli, Nathmal ki Haveli, Salim Singh ki Haveli, Gadisar Lake, Bada Bagh, Lodurva and Kuldhara.

faq.q: Is Jaisalmer Fort a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.a: Yes. It is one of six forts inscribed in 2013 as the Hill Forts of Rajasthan, with Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron and Amber.

faq.q: Do people still live inside Jaisalmer Fort?
faq.a: Yes. It is often called a living fort because several thousand people live and work inside its walls, which raises real conservation questions about water, drainage and new construction.

faq.q: Is Kuldhara worth visiting with students?
faq.a: Yes, if framed historically. It is an abandoned village of Paliwal Brahmins where you can see house plans, streets and a temple. The many ghost stories about it are folklore, which itself can be a discussion point.

faq.q: How long does a Jaisalmer heritage walk take?
faq.a: About three to four hours for the fort and havelis on foot. Add half a day by vehicle for Bada Bagh, Lodurva and Kuldhara.

posts.hook: People still live inside Jaisalmer Fort.
posts.caption: Founded in 1156, the fort is a UNESCO site and a neighbourhood at once. That is wonderful, and a real conservation problem: water and drains do not mix well with 850 year old walls.

posts.hook: Go to the Jain temples first thing.
posts.caption: Visiting hours are short, usually mornings. Look at the brackets and ceilings, carved in the same yellow sandstone as the fort walls.
